problems.title: Nested List Weight Sum II
problems.summary: You get a nested list of integers. An integer's weight is maxDepth − depth + 1, so the deepest integers weigh 1 and top-level ones weigh the most. Return the sum of every integer times its weight.
problems.idea: BFS level by level; keep a running sum of all integers seen so far and add it to the total at each level — deeper items get counted fewer times.
problems.full:
You're given a list nestedList whose elements are either integers or other lists. Those lists can themselves contain integers or lists, nested to any depth.

An integer's depth is how many lists it sits inside. Integers directly in nestedList have depth 1, integers inside one inner list have depth 2, and so on. Let maxDepth be the largest depth of any integer.

Each integer's weight is maxDepth − depth + 1. The deepest integers weigh 1 and top-level integers weigh the most (the reverse of the original Nested List Weight Sum). Return the sum of every integer multiplied by its weight.

You work through the provided NestedInteger interface:

  • isInteger(): true if this element holds a single integer
  • getInteger(): the integer, if it holds one
  • getList(): the nested list, if it holds a list

Example 1

Input:  [[1,1],2,[1,1]]
Output: 8
maxDepth = 2. The four 1s are at depth 2, weight 1 → 4.
The 2 is at depth 1, weight 2 → 4. Total 8.

Example 2

Input:  [1,[4,[6]]]
Output: 17
maxDepth = 3. 1×3 + 4×2 + 6×1 = 17.

Example 3

Input:  [[], 5]
Output: 5
The empty list holds no integers, so maxDepth = 1 and 5 has weight 1.

Constraints (approx.)

  • 1 to 50 elements in each list
  • Integer values from −100 to 100
  • Nesting depth at most 50
tests: depthSumInverse([1, [[]]])  — empty lists deeper than every integer don't count toward maxDepth
depthSumInverse([[1], [2], [3, [4]]])  — several branches of different depth

problems.title: Max Stack
problems.summary: Design a stack that also supports finding and removing its maximum: push(x), pop(), top(), peekMax(), and popMax(). If several elements share the max, popMax removes the one closest to the top.
problems.example: push 5, push 1, push 5 → top()=5, popMax()=5, top()=1, peekMax()=5, pop()=1, top()=5
problems.idea: Doubly linked list for stack order + TreeMap<val, Deque<Node>> for max; popMax unlinks from the middle. O(log n).
problems.full:
Design a stack that, in addition to the usual operations, can find and remove its largest element. Implement MaxStack:

  • MaxStack(): creates an empty stack
  • void push(int x): puts x on top
  • int pop(): removes the top element and returns it
  • int top(): returns the top element without removing it
  • int peekMax(): returns the largest element without removing it
  • int popMax(): removes the largest element and returns it. If several elements share the largest value, remove the one closest to the top

Aim for top in O(1) and every other operation in O(log n).

Example

push(5)     stack: [5]
push(1)     stack: [5, 1]
push(5)     stack: [5, 1, 5]        (top is on the right)
top()     → 5
popMax()  → 5   stack: [5, 1]       (the top-most 5 is removed)
top()     → 1
peekMax() → 5
pop()     → 1   stack: [5]
top()     → 5

Constraints (approx.)

  • Values from −107 to 107
  • Up to 105 operations
  • pop, top, peekMax and popMax are only called when the stack isn't empty

problems.title: Read N Characters Given read4 II - Call Multiple Times
problems.summary: You can only read a file through read4(buf4), which copies up to 4 characters into buf4 and returns how many it copied. Implement read(buf, n) that copies up to n characters into buf and returns the count. read may be called many times, so characters read4 fetched but you didn't return yet must be kept for the next call.
problems.idea: Keep a 4-char buffer + pointer + count as fields across calls; drain the buffer first, call read4 when empty, stop at n or EOF.
problems.full:
You can only read a file through a provided method read4(buf4). Each call copies up to 4 characters, starting from where the previous call stopped, into the array buf4 and returns how many it copied. It returns fewer than 4 near the end of the file, and 0 once the file is exhausted. You can't access the file in any other way.

Implement read(buf, n): copy up to n characters from the file into buf and return how many were copied (fewer than n only if the file runs out).

The catch: read can be called several times, and each call must continue exactly where the previous one stopped. read4 always fetches in chunks of 4, so a call may fetch characters it doesn't need yet. Keep those leftovers in your object and hand them out first on the next call.

Example 1

file = "abc"
read(buf, 1) → 1    buf starts with "a"
read(buf, 2) → 2    "bc"
read(buf, 1) → 0    end of file

Example 2

file = "abcdefgh"
read(buf, 5) → 5    "abcde"   (read4 fetched "abcd", then "efgh"; "fgh" is left over)
read(buf, 2) → 2    "fg"      (served from the leftovers, no read4 call needed)
read(buf, 4) → 1    "h"

Constraints (approx.)

  • The file has up to about 500 characters (letters and digits)
  • 1 ≤ n ≤ about 500 per call; buf always has room for n characters
tests: file "abcd": read(4), read(1) — exact multiple of 4
file "abc": read(10) — n larger than the file
file "abcdefghij": read(1) ×4 then read(10) — many tiny reads
file "abcdefg": read(3), read(2), read(2) — reads across a read4 boundary

def read_calls(file, ns):
    _file["s"] = file; _file["p"] = 0
    s = Solution(); out = []
    for n in ns:
        buf = [""] * (n + 4)
        c = s.read(buf, n)
        out.append("".join(buf[:c]))
    return out

problems.full:
Design a class that's built once from a list of words and then answers many queries about it. Implement WordDistance:

  • WordDistance(String[] wordsDict): stores the list
  • int shortest(String word1, String word2): returns the smallest |i − j| such that wordsDict[i] = word1 and wordsDict[j] = word2

Both words are in the list, and word1 ≠ word2. A word can appear many times. Because shortest is called repeatedly, preprocess so each query is fast.

shortest("coding", "practice") → 3     (index 3 vs index 0)
shortest("makes", "coding")    → 1     ("makes" at 1 and 4; "coding" at 3 → |4 − 3| = 1)

  • Up to 3 × 104 words, each up to 10 lowercase letters
  • Up to 5,000 calls to shortest

problems.title: Closest Binary Search Tree Value II
problems.summary: Given a BST, a target (a decimal) and k, return the k values in the tree closest to the target, in any order.
problems.idea: Inorder walk keeping a size-k deque (drop the farther end): O(n). Predecessor/successor stacks: O(log n + k).
problems.full:
Given the root of a binary search tree, a target value (a decimal number) and an integer k, return the k values in the tree that are closest to target, meaning they have the smallest |value − target|. Return them in any order.

The input guarantees there is exactly one set of k closest values, so there are no ties at the boundary.

Example 1

Tree:         4
            /   \
           2     5
          / \
         1   3
target = 3.714286, k = 2
Output: [4, 3]       (distances 0.29 and 0.71)

Example 2

Tree: [1], target = 0.0, k = 1
Output: [1]

Follow-up: if the BST is balanced, can you beat O(n)? Aim for about O(log n + k).

Constraints (approx.)

  • 1 to 104 nodes
  • 1 ≤ k ≤ number of nodes
  • Node values from 0 to 109
  • target from −109 to 109

problems.title: Copy List with Random Pointer
problems.summary: Each node of a linked list has next and an extra random pointer (to any node, or null). Return a deep copy, where the new nodes point only to other new nodes.
problems.example: [[7,null],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]]  (value, index that random points to) → an identical, separate list
problems.idea: Map old → new in two passes; or interleave copies (A→A'→B→B') then split for O(1) space.
tests: single node whose random points to itself
duplicate values: copy must follow pointers, not values
problems.py_post:
@@PYHELPERS@@

def RL(pairs):
    nodes = [Node(v) for v, _ in pairs]
    for i, n in enumerate(nodes):
        n.next = nodes[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(nodes) else None
        r = pairs[i][1]
        n.random = nodes[r] if r is not None else None
    return nodes[0] if nodes else None
def RA(head):
    nodes, n = [], head
    while n and len(nodes) < 100000:
        nodes.append(n); n = n.next
    idx = {id(x): i for i, x in enumerate(nodes)}
    return [[x.val, idx.get(id(x.random)) if x.random else None] for x in nodes]
def no_shared(a, b):
    seen, n = set(), a
    while n: seen.add(id(n)); n = n.next
    n = b
    while n:
        if id(n) in seen: return False
        n = n.next
    return True

    h = RL([[7,None],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]])
    c = Solution().copyRandomList(h)
    got = [RA(c), no_shared(h, c)]
    return got

problems.title: Alien Dictionary
problems.summary: Words are sorted in an unknown alphabet. Derive one valid letter order, or "" if the input is inconsistent.
problems.full:
An alien language uses the lowercase English letters, but in an unknown order. You're given a list of words from its dictionary, sorted according to that alien order.

Return a string of all the distinct letters that appear in the words, arranged in an order consistent with the list. If several orders work, return any of them. If no order can be consistent, return "".

"Sorted" works like a normal dictionary. Compare two words letter by letter, and the first position where they differ decides which comes first. If one word is a prefix of the other, the shorter word comes first.

The input is invalid (return "") when:

  • the letter rules contradict each other (a cycle such as a < b and b < a), or
  • a longer word comes before its own prefix, e.g. ["abc", "ab"].

Example 1

Input:  ["wrt","wrf","er","ett","rftt"]
Output: "wertf"
wrt/wrf → t before f;  wrf/er → w before e;  er/ett → r before t;  ett/rftt → e before r.

Example 2

Input:  ["z","x"]
Output: "zx"

Example 3

Input:  ["z","x","z"]
Output: ""        (z before x and x before z: impossible)

Constraints (approx.)

  • 1 to 100 words, each 1 to 100 lowercase letters

A handy equivalent: a graph is a tree exactly when it has n − 1 edges and is connected.

Output: true

  • No self-loops and no repeated edges

  • String encode(List<String> strs): turns the list into one string
